source_read: PMC HTML, PMC5944879 (Am J Public Health 2018;108(6):777–781), read in full in the reader's own browser tab (title confirmed): abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 1–3, discussion with Limitations, Public Health Implications, references. No figures. Table 1 and Table 3 percentages and 95% intervals recomputed by the reader (Wald intervals match the printed ones).

claims.overstatement: No overstatement of this source; the claim is more cautious than the authors (it says the protocol counted toxicology markers and could only add deaths, where the authors judge the enhanced count more accurate with near certainty). Minor: the Maryland comparator is the authors' search of certificate text for the word heroin, not a published coded statistic.
claims.note: Every Horon number in the statement and magnitude checks: 1,130 against 2,182 (28.6% and 55.1% of 3,957); 1,052 added = 804 + 193 + 55 (76.4%, 18.3%, 5.2%); 51.8% (49.7–53.9) of protocol deaths named heroin on the certificate, 45.7% in 2012 to 56.3% in 2015, 41.9% at 55 or older, 35.1% of women, 25.9% (18.5–33.3) of Black women; the four criteria, the agencies and the limitation on the 55 are as the claim states. Points for the editor: (1) the Maryland comparator is the authors' own text search of OCME cause-of-death entries for heroin (Methods 2nd paragraph), not a published statistic; 'official counts built from death certificates' is fair, since official counts come from the same entries, but the claim could say the certificates themselves were searched; (2) Table 2 prints 1,042 for morphine-certified records with scene evidence, while the text gives 804 twice and 1,052 − 193 − 55 = 804, so the claim's 804 is right; (3) the protocol excluded deaths whose scene notes pointed to prescription morphine, a guard against over-counting the claim could mention; (4) 'Black women' = non-Hispanic Black women (35 of 135); Hispanic women, 0 of 4, are rightly not mentioned; (5) Horon names time from use to specimen collection (not to death) and does not mention stored samples, so those parts of the 'why heroin is missed' sentence rest on Stam et al.; (6) the 3,957 total is defined only by the cause-of-death terms used to pull records (citing a state report), with no intent or residence rule, so 'a total not defined in the paper' is fair; (7) nothing was validated against an independent standard, and the authors attribute the 2012–2015 rise in certificate naming to recommendations already being implemented, so the gap was narrowing.

anchors.extracted: A death counts as heroin-related on a certificate only if the certifier writes heroin. Reasons it may not be written (from cited literature): nonspecific causes such as narcotic intoxication or drug overdose; time between use and specimen collection, route, chronic use and analysis quality; heroin's very short half-life, so it is rarely detected; morphine and 6-monoacetylmorphine are far more likely to be found, so morphine intoxication may be certified even when outside information points to heroin.

Maryland's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner investigates violent, suicidal, accidental, suspicious and unexpected deaths and certifies the cause, which is the certifier's opinion and may vary between certifiers. Standard approach: cause-of-death sections of OCME certificates, 2012–2015, searched for the word heroin.

Enhanced protocol built by the Vital Statistics Administration, OCME, the Maryland Poison Center and the Behavioral Health Administration; all OCME records with poisoning, intoxication, toxicity, overdose and similar cause terms reviewed (cause, toxicology, scene notes). Heroin-related if any of: (1) heroin on the certificate; (2) 6-monoacetylmorphine on toxicology; (3) quinine with morphine or free morphine (quinine described as often added to heroin); (4) morphine or no specific substance on the certificate plus scene notes suggesting heroin (e.g. a person known to use heroin found with paraphernalia, or witnessed use). Not counted if scene notes suggested prescription morphine. No step judges whether heroin caused the death.

Certificates named heroin in 1,130 deaths 2012–2015; enhanced protocol 2,182, about twice as many. Of 3,957 total overdose deaths: 1,130 (28.6%) against 2,182 (55.1%); by year 179/392 of 799 (2012), 221/464 of 858, 309/578 of 1,041, 421/748 of 1,259 (2015).

1,052 deaths added by the protocol; overlapping sources: 6-monoacetylmorphine 136, morphine with quinine 892, morphine or free morphine with scene evidence 998; text: 804 records certified morphine (alone or with other substances), all with scene evidence. Table 2 prints 1,042 for the morphine-certified row, inconsistent with the text's 804.

Of the 1,052 records without heroin on the certificate: morphine certified 804 (76.4%), no specific substance (e.g. narcotic or opioid intoxication) 193 (18.3%), another substance 55 (5.2%). Share of protocol heroin deaths named on certificates rose from 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015).

Certificates named heroin in 1,130 of 2,182 protocol heroin deaths, 51.8% (95% CI 49.7–53.9); 2012 45.7% (40.7–50.6), 2015 56.3% (52.7–59.8); under 25 58.2%, 55 or older 41.9% (36.6–47.1); non-Hispanic White 53.5%, non-Hispanic Black 47.0%; men 56.8%, women 35.1% (30.9–39.3); non-Hispanic Black women 25.9% (35/135; 18.5–33.3); Hispanic men 77.3%, Hispanic women 0 of 4. Table excludes 1 unknown age, 3 unknown race, 1 unknown sex.

Some added deaths may not have been heroin-related: a small share of those certified as morphine intoxication, and some of the 55 with another substance certified, where the certifier may have judged heroin present but not directly related to death. The authors nonetheless judge the enhanced count 'almost certainly' more accurate; no validation against an independent standard is reported.

National expert recommendations: list every physiologically significant drug and the parent drug rather than the metabolite when toxicology or scene findings support it (e.g. heroin rather than morphine). Implementation already under way in Maryland, where the certificate share rose from 45.7% (2012) to 56.3% (2015).
